Know the line

“It was only a joke” is not a defence.

The Act looks at whether conduct was unwelcome, not whether it was meant to hurt. Most complaints begin with behaviour someone thought was harmless.

Behaviour the Act treats as harassment

  • Physical contact and advances
  • A demand or request for sexual favours
  • Sexually coloured remarks
  • Showing pornography
  • Any other unwelcome physical, verbal or non-verbal conduct of a sexual nature

Situations that make it harassment too

  • An implied or explicit promise of preferential treatment at work
  • An implied or explicit threat of detrimental treatment
  • A threat about present or future employment status
  • Interference with work, or creating an intimidating, offensive or hostile environment
  • Humiliating treatment likely to affect health or safety

Where it happens

  • Offices and branches
  • Client sites and off-sites
  • Employer-provided transport
  • WhatsApp groups and video calls
  • Work-from-home setups

Your legal duties

A committee on paper is not compliance.

The Act holds the employer accountable, not just the Internal Committee (ICC). Here is what you must do every year, and how we help you do each part.

What non-compliance really costs

Up to ₹50,000 for the first offence, double the penalty for repeats, and possible cancellation of your business licence or registration. Add to that the damage to trust, talent and reputation.

What a valid ICC looks like

A presiding officer who is a senior woman employee, at least two employee members committed to the cause of women or with legal knowledge, and one external member. At least half the members must be women.

01

Build

  • A written anti-harassment policy
  • An Internal Committee at every office or branch
  • An external member on the committee
02

Communicate

  • Display the penal consequences and committee details
  • Run regular awareness programmes
  • Orient ICC members
03

Report

  • Treat harassment as misconduct and act on recommendations
  • Include PoSH details in the annual report
  • File with the District Officer
  • Update SHe-Box where applicable

When a complaint comes in

Six stages. Fixed deadlines. Every one defensible.

A missed deadline or a one-sided inquiry can be overturned on appeal. We prepare your committee to get every stage right: fairly, confidentially and on time.

  1. 01

    Complaint

    Within 3 months (extendable by 3)Written complaint to the ICC from the date of the incident.How we help: Clear complaint channels and an intake form.

  2. 02

    Conciliation

    OptionalAt the complainant’s request, the ICC may try to settle the matter. No monetary settlement is allowed.How we help: Guidance on when conciliation is appropriate.

  3. 03

    Inquiry

    Within 90 daysA fair inquiry following natural justice: both parties heard, evidence recorded.How we help: Inquiry planning, hearing protocols and documentation templates.

  4. 04

    Report

    Within 10 daysFindings and recommendations shared with the employer and both parties once the inquiry ends.How we help: Report-writing support so findings are reasoned and clear.

  5. 05

    Action

    Within 60 daysThe employer acts on the committee’s recommendations.How we help: Advice on proportionate, policy-aligned action.

  6. 06

    Appeal

    Within 90 daysEither party may appeal against the recommendations before the appellate authority.How we help: Records that hold up on appeal.

FAQs

Straight answers for HR teams

Not sure what applies to your organisation? Ask us — you'll get a clear answer, not legal jargon.

Book a PoSH consultation
Who needs to comply?

Every organisation in India with 10 or more employees must constitute an Internal Committee and meet the requirements of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

Why do we need an external member?

The Act requires one for independence. They bring outside expertise and make the committee’s findings more credible.

How often should training be held?

The Act asks for regular awareness programmes without fixing a frequency. Best practice is at least once a year, plus induction for new joiners and refreshers for ICC members.

Who is covered, only permanent employees?

No. Permanent, contract, temporary, ad hoc, interns and trainees, and visitors to your premises.

What if we have fewer than 10 employees?

No ICC is required. Complaints go to the district-level Local Committee. We still recommend a written policy.

Does the Act protect men as well?

The statute protects women. Many organisations adopt gender-neutral policies so every employee has a fair route.

Is the complaint kept confidential?

Yes. The Act prohibits disclosing the complaint, the parties’ identities and the inquiry proceedings.

Can PoSH training be conducted online?

Yes, the Act does not prescribe a format. For ICC members we recommend live or hybrid mock inquiries.

General information, not legal advice.
